newsitem.title: USA: Fed passes 12 quiet months, markets applaud.
newsitem.headline: Fed passes 12 quiet months, markets applaud.

text.p: Among the praise heaped on Federal Reserve policy-makers in recent months, perhaps the most telling testament is that the central bank has held short-term interest rates steady for a year.

The last time rates were steady at least that long was from early September 1992 to early February 1994. Since Jan. 31, 1996, when the Fed cut two key short-term rates in a bid to boost economic growth, the central bank's policy-makers have shown a degree of patience that is paying handsome dividends, economists and former Fed governors said.
The Fed's handling of the economy, via the short-term rates that it controls, has all but stopped inflation in its tracks.

"I give the Fed most of the credit for where we are now. They have fostered an environment in which inflation expectations have been greatly diminished," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.
"I'm very impressed by this board of governors. They have done the best job that I can think of since the 1960s," said Preston Martin, vice chairman at the Fed from 1982 to 1986.

The lack of worry about inflation, which has hovered near 3 percent since 1991 as measured by the Consumer Price Index, reflects confidence in the Fed's readiness to respond to latent price pressures, analysts said.
Free from fear of rapid price growth, American workers have grudgingly adapted to slower wage growth than that seen as recently as the 1980s.
Consumers have become smarter and thriftier, while many businesses have been unwilling or unable to raise prices significantly.

"The Fed is benefiting from its heightened credibility. People don't act in inflationary ways," said Lyle Gramley, a former Federal Reserve Board governor and now a consulting economist to the Mortgage Bankers Association of America.

Yet the Fed's ride has had a few bumps. When strong job growth last July and August dropped the unemployment rate to a seven-year low of 5.1 percent, many pundits warned that inflation was looming and clamoured for a Fed rate hike.
At several policy-setting meetings last year, Minneapolis Fed President Gary Stern urged his colleagues to boost rates right away, citing the risk that rising wages could fuel a pickup in inflation.

But in October the Labour Department said the economy lost 40,000 jobs in September, signalling to many that the Fed was right in holding rates steady. Higher rates dampen inflation by restraining overall economic growth.
"They've been sitting on a knife edge since the middle of last year, but they've gotten away with it. Looking back, they did the right thing by waiting," said Gramley.
The Fed's current patience would appear to contrast with the "pre-emptive" stance it has exhibited in past cycles.

For example, in response to a spurt of economic growth in late 1993, the Fed raised rates on Feb. 4, 1994, and another six times after that. In hindsight, the Fed acted correctly, economists said, helping to slow economic growth from 3.5 percent in 1994 to a more sustainable 2.0 percent in 1995.

Economists estimate that Gross Domestic Product, the broadest measure of the nation's economy, will grow about 2.5 percent this year after rising about 3 percent in 1996. Many expect the Fed to start raising rates by mid-year.
But Martin and other pro-growth advocates believe the Fed should hold its fire, giving the economy the benefit of the doubt.

After all, recent economic growth has yet to boost inflation significantly and forecasts for future price gains could easily miss the mark, said Martin, now chairman at HomeVest Financial Services Inc. in San Francisco.
He said the Fed's recent "Beige Book" summaries of economic conditions have shown widespread growth in the 12 Fed districts but few signs of price pressures.
"The word they beat to death in the latest Beige Book was 'moderate' when describing growth. You'd think the same guy wrote all 12 (district) reports," Martin said.
But more mainstream economists see at least a small rise in inflation already baked in the cake.
Labour Department data showed wages rose 3.3 percent in 1996, suggesting to some economists that the tight job market might force wages higher still and lead to a pickup in inflation.

"While we haven't seen much pickup in inflation, there is a risk that the Fed would overstay its hand in not doing anything. We all know once inflation starts to pick up, it's very difficult to reverse," said Mellon Bank's Berner.
"Strong medicine clearly isn't required, but that doesn't mean no medicine is required. If the Fed does take some action, inflation will stay near 3 percent," he said.
